diagnostic_evidence.quote: However, in our analysis we do not require the \emph{empirical Gram matrix} $\wh{\bm{G}}_{NM}$  to be invertible.

issues.failure_explanation: When $\wh{\bm{G}}_{NM}$ is singular (e.g. when $M < N$ or when sample points do not hit the support of some basis functions), $\wh{\Psi}$ is linearly dependent in $\wh{\Ff}_M$. The induced mapping $\wh{\Aa}$ is defined by $\wh{\Aa}\wh{\psi} := \wh{\Aa\psi}$, but this is not well-defined on $\wh{\Ff}_{NM}$: if $\sum_{i=1}^N c_i \wh{\psi}_i = 0$, that only means $\sum_{i=1}^N c_i \psi_i(\bm{x}_m) = 0$ for all $m$, which does not imply $\sum_{i=1}^N c_i (\Aa\psi_i)( m{x}_m) = 0$ (for differential operators, a function can vanish at sample points while its derivative does not). Furthermore, the proof uses Lemma A.1 by asserting that $\sum_{i=1}^N c_i [\wh{\bm{C}}_{NM}]_{ij} = \langle \wh{\Aa} \sum_{i=1}^N c_i \wh{\psi}_i, \wh{\psi}_j \rangle = 0$, which is false. In general, $\wh{ m{A}}_{NM}$ can map the zero element of $\wh{\Ff}_{NM}$ to a non-zero element, meaning $\wh{\Aa}_{NM}$ is not even a well-defined operator on $\wh{\Ff}_{NM}$.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3 to the regime where $\wh{\bm{G}}_{NM}$ is invertible (or for $M \ge m_0$ as established in Lemma 3.6), withdrawing the claim that invertibility of $\wh{\bm{G}}_{NM}$ is not needed.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3 fail in the advertised regime where $\wh{\bm{G}}_{NM}$ is not invertible.
issues.title: Empirical projection operator is ill-defined when empirical Gram matrix is singular
issues.why_classification: Requiring invertibility of $\wh{\bm{G}}_{NM}$ repairs the operator definition and proof but withdraws an explicitly advertised regime/contribution of Section 3 without affecting the downstream asymptotic results.

diagnostic_evidence.quote:
Furthermore, if $f \in \Ff_\infty$ and
	$\norm{(\Pp_{\Ff_N}- Id)\phi}_\Ff = \mathcal{O}( N^{-\alpha})$ for all $\phi \in \Ff$

issues.failure_explanation: In an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space $\Ff$, it is impossible for the orthogonal projections onto finite-dimensional subspaces $\Ff_N$ to satisfy $\|\Pp_{\Ff_N} \phi - \phi\|_\Ff = \mathcal{O}(N^{-\alpha})$ for all $\phi \in \Ff$. By the Uniform Boundedness Principle, if $\sup_N N^\alpha \|(\rm{Id} - \Pp_{\Ff_N})\phi\| < \infty$ for all $\phi \in \Ff$, then $\|\rm{Id} - \Pp_{\Ff_N}\| \to 0$ in the operator norm. However, since $\Ff_N$ is a proper finite-dimensional subspace, $\|\rm{Id} - \Pp_{\Ff_N}\| = 1$ for all $N$. Therefore, the hypothesis is vacuous on any infinite-dimensional state space.

failure_location.quote:
Consider $\Psi_N$ satisfying Assumption \ref{assumption} and such that $ \norm{\Pp_{\Ff_N} \phi-\phi}_\Ff = \mathcal{O}(N^{-\alpha})
	$ for all $\phi\in \Ff$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the condition 'for all $\phi \in \Ff$' with the requirement that the rate holds for $\phi = \Aa\psi$ (or for $\phi$ in a dense subspace of sufficiently regular functions).
issues.overall_effect: The rate guarantees in Corollary 4.4 and Theorem 5.3 rest on a vacuous premise that no dictionary in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space can satisfy.
issues.title: Impossible uniform convergence rate on entire Hilbert space
issues.why_classification: Restricting the rate condition to the relevant observable $\phi = \Aa\psi$ or a smoothness class is a standard, local condition that preserves the asymptotic rate and conclusions.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Now, by definition of $\tl{\mathbb{P}}$, we have that $\tl{p}_N\tl{\mathbb{P}}\leq \mathbb{P}$.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof of Proposition 5.5 suffers from two fatal defects: (1) Equation (22) asserts that $\bm{G}_N = \E[\bm{g}\bm{g}^\dagger]$ where $ m{g}_m = \Psi_N(\bm{x}_m) + \bm{\eta}_N^m$. But because $ m{\eta}_N^m$ is non-trivial random noise, $\E[\bm{g}\bm{g}^\dagger] = \bm{G}_N + \operatorname{Cov}(\bm{\eta}_N^m) \ne \bm{G}_N$. The noise variance introduces an asymptotic bias: $\tl{ m{G}}_{NM} \to \bm{G}_N + \bm{\Sigma}_\eta$ as $M \to \infty$. Hence, $\bm{S^G}_m$ does not have mean zero, Bernstein's inequality is inapplicable, and $\|\tl{\Aa}_{NM} - \Aa_N\|$ does not converge to 0 as $M \to \infty$, contradicting the bound for arbitrarily small $\delta$. (2) The conditional probability $\tl{\mathbb{P}}$ conditions on the event that $|(\bm{\eta}_N^m, \bm{\xi}_N^m)|^2 \le \tl{\gamma}_N$ holds simultaneously for all $m=1,\dots,M$. Since samples are independent, the probability of this conditioning event is $(\tl{p}_N)^M$, not $\tl{p}_N$. The inequality $\tl{p}_N \tl{\mathbb{P}} \le \mathbb{P}$ is invalid because $(\tl{p}_N)^M \to 0$ as $M \to \infty$.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must employ a de-biasing technique (such as instrumental variables or total least squares) or formulate bounds on the error relative to the biased limit rather than $\Aa_N$, and correctly account for the sample-size dependence in the noise concentration.
issues.overall_effect: Proposition 5.5 and Theorem 5.6 are invalid. The estimator $\tl{\Aa}_{NM}$ suffers from a persistent errors-in-variables bias and does not converge to $\Aa_N$ as $M \to \infty$.
issues.title: Noise bias in empirical Gram matrix and invalid conditioning in error bound
issues.why_classification: The error bound for noisy data completely fails due to an unaddressed structural bias and an invalid probabilistic conditioning; correcting it requires an entirely different estimator or withdrawing the convergence-to-zero claim in the noisy regime.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The first part follows from $\left(\lambda_{NM}\right)$ and $\big(f_{NM}\big)$ being bounded sequences of $\C$ and $\Ff_N\subset \Dd$, respectively.

issues.failure_explanation: Theorem 6.2 claims that for any sequence $(\lambda_N, f_N)$ of eigenpairs of $\Aa_N$, there exists a subsequence such that $\lambda_{N_i} \to \lambda \in \C$. The proof justifies the existence of a convergent subsequence of eigenvalues by claiming that because each individual $\Aa_N$ is bounded on $\Ff_N$, the sequence $(\lambda_N)_{N=1}^\infty$ is bounded. This inference is false: for unbounded operators $\Aa$ (such as generators of semigroups, which the paper specifically focuses on), the eigenvalues of the Galerkin approximations $\Aa_N$ can diverge to infinity as $N \to \infty$. When $\lambda_N \to \infty$, no subsequence converges in $\C$.

failure_location.quote: Additionally, for each $N$, $\Aa_N$ is bounded. Thus, the sequence of eigenvalues $(\lambda_{N})$ is also bounded and has a convergent subsequence.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the explicit hypothesis that the sequence of eigenvalues $(\lambda_N)_{N=1}^\infty$ is bounded in $\C$ (or restrict attention to bounded operators $\Aa$).
issues.overall_effect: The existence of convergent subsequences of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions in Theorem 6.2 and Theorem 6.3 is unsupported and false for unbounded operators when eigenvalues escape to infinity.
issues.title: Unjustified eigenvalue boundedness and convergence for unbounded operators
issues.why_classification: Adding the condition that the sequence of eigenvalues is bounded restores the Bolzano-Weierstrass argument without altering the remaining proof architecture, but narrows the theorem by excluding sequences of eigenvalues that escape to infinity.
